prompt.context: Our client, High Q Plastics, is an automotive parts supplier in the US. They primarily manufacture and sell plastic injection-molded parts — such as grills, door handles, and decorative trim — to automotive customers. The client has two primary revenue sources: large automotive OEMs and the aftermarket segment. The client has recently seen declining profits, primarily due to increased price competition from new overseas competitors in China. Annual profits have declined from $50M to $20M over the last few years.
prompt.question: What is the reason behind the declining profitability? How can High Q improve profits? Can they reach $100M in profit by 2014?

clarifying_info.q: What is happening with overall automotive sales?
clarifying_info.a: Automotive sales overall are still growing steadily, driven by emerging markets, but automotive manufacturing is leaving the United States.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's competitive position?
clarifying_info.a: The client is currently one of the market leaders, has US-based manufacturing, and its products are higher quality than Chinese competitors'. Revenues have slowly declined for the last fifteen years.
Automotive OEM customers are looking to reduce cost, driving increased price competition among parts suppliers.

exhibits.title: Plant-Level P&L (2010 baseline)
exhibits.shows: A table showing 2010 financials (in $M USD) for four US plants — Plant A, B, C, and D — broken down by Revenues, Labor, Material, Overhead, and Net Profits.

exhibits.title: 2010 U.S. Automotive Sales by Segment
exhibits.shows: A pie chart of 2010 U.S. automotive sales by vehicle type, with a note on total market size.

exhibits.title: OEM Truck/SUV Market Share 2010–2014
exhibits.shows: A grouped bar chart comparing each major OEM's share of the Truck/SUV segment in 2010 vs. 2014, with additional information about High Q's relationship with Toyota.

data.additional: High Q supplies 70% of Toyota's business. Avg. price of High Q products sold to Toyota = $20.

framework: Industry analysis: assess sales volume trends, OEM vs. aftermarket demand split and growth, and relative profitability of each segment
Competitor analysis: identify overseas (Chinese) competitors, compare relative market share, pricing, cost structure, and quality/technology positioning
Revenue deep-dive: examine how client prices have changed across customers and product lines, and whether price declines are uniform
Cost deep-dive: identify trends in labor costs, raw material costs, and SG&A; compare cost structure vs. competitors
Profit model: Profit = Q × (P − VC) − FC; understand each lever — volume, price, variable cost, fixed cost — to size improvement opportunities
Feasibility assessment: quantify impact of proposed initiatives against $100M profit target

questions.prompt: Q1: What key questions would you ask an industry expert to understand the reasons behind High Q's declining profits?
questions.guidance: Candidate should generate MECE diagnostic questions across four buckets: (1) Industry — volume trends, OEM vs. aftermarket mix, segment profitability; (2) Competitors — who they are, market share, price levels, cost structure, technology/quality advantage; (3) Revenue — how client prices have changed, whether declines are across all customers and products; (4) Costs — labor and material cost trends vs. competitors.

questions.prompt: Q2: The CEO wants to know if $100M in annual profit is achievable by 2014. What information would you need to determine this?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the profit formula: Profit = Q × (P − VC) − FC. Therefore they need annual quantity sold, selling price (and how it is changing), and the breakdown of fixed vs. variable costs. Candidate should flag that current profit is $20M, so a 5× increase requires either large volume gains, price increases, significant cost cuts, or some combination.

steps: Requires knowing Q, P, VC breakdown, and FC to model any scenario
math.answer: Need volume, price, variable cost, and fixed cost data to quantify feasibility.

questions.prompt: Q3: What ways can you think of to increase revenues and reduce costs?
questions.guidance: Revenue ideas: segment customers by price sensitivity to defend margins; increase marketing and sales effort in the aftermarket segment (less price-competitive than OEM); negotiate long-term contracts with OEM customers to lock in volume. Cost-reduction ideas: find alternative/lower-cost material sources; invest in process automation to reduce labor; consolidate multiple US plants to reduce SG&A and overhead; relocate closer to customers to reduce transportation costs.

questions.prompt: Q4: The client plans to implement lean manufacturing across all four plants. In 2014 they expect to produce 80% of 2010 volumes, reduce prices by 10%, and achieve 20% savings on raw materials and 30% savings on labor. Overhead is unchanged. What is the change in profits from 2010 to 2014? (Use Exhibit 1)
questions.guidance: Key insight: revenues, labor, and material all scale with volume (80%), THEN apply the additional lean savings on top. Overhead does not change. Revenue also takes a 10% price cut on top of the 80% volume = effective revenue factor of 0.72. Candidate must not forget to apply the volume reduction to costs before applying lean savings. Total 2014 profit ≈ $28M — still far below the $100M target, which should prompt the candidate to flag that the goal is unlikely achievable through lean manufacturing alone.

math.setup: 2014 Revenue per plant = 2010 Revenue × 0.80 (volume) × 0.90 (price) = $100M × 0.72 = $72M. Labor 2014 = 2010 Labor × 0.80 × 0.70 (30% lean saving). Material 2014 = 2010 Material × 0.80 × 0.80 (20% lean saving). Overhead 2014 = 2010 Overhead (unchanged).
math.answer: Total 2014 profit ≈ $28M, up $8M from $20M. Still far below $100M target.

questions.prompt: Q5: Using Exhibits 2 and 3, analyze OEM competitive dynamics to predict any increase in High Q profits from increased sales to Toyota.
questions.guidance: Candidate should use the Trucks/SUV segment share (20% of total market) and Toyota's dramatic share gain (10% to 40%) to calculate incremental High Q revenue. Then apply High Q's 70% supply share and $20 average price to get dollar revenue impact. Strong candidates will note this is a revenue increase only — margin impact depends on cost structure.

math.setup: Step 1: size 2010 Trucks/SUV market. Step 2: calculate Toyota unit volumes in 2010 and 2014. Step 3: apply High Q supplier share and price.
steps: Toyota 2014 Truck/SUV units = 3.2M × 40% = 1,280,000 (assuming total market flat at 16M)
High Q units sold to Toyota 2010 = 320,000 × 70% = 224,000
High Q units sold to Toyota 2014 = 1,280,000 × 70% = 896,000
math.answer: High Q can expect approximately $13.4M in incremental revenue from Toyota's Truck/SUV market share gain.

brainstorming.prompt: What ways can you think of to increase revenues and/or reduce costs for High Q Plastics?

categories.name: Reduce Costs
ideas: Find alternative or lower-cost raw material sources to reduce material spend
Invest in process automation to reduce labor costs
Consolidate the four US manufacturing plants to reduce SG&A and overhead
Relocate plants closer to key customers to reduce transportation costs
Implement lean manufacturing to eliminate waste across production lines

categories.name: Increase Revenue
ideas: Segment OEM customers by price sensitivity to protect margins on less price-sensitive accounts
Increase marketing and sales investment in the aftermarket segment, which faces less price pressure from Chinese competitors
Negotiate long-term supply contracts with OEM customers to secure volume
Pursue Toyota as a growth account given its rising Truck/SUV market share
Diversify into plastic injection-molded parts for non-automotive industries with less price competition

recommendation: Yes, High Q should implement lean manufacturing across all four plants — it improves profit from $20M to approximately $28M
However, lean manufacturing alone will not achieve the CEO's $100M profit target by 2014; the gap remains approximately $72M
risks: Volume continues to decline beyond 80% forecast as automotive OEMs source more from Chinese suppliers
Price competition intensifies further, eroding the 10% price cut assumption
Lean implementation costs and disruption could reduce near-term profit before savings materialize
next_steps: Consolidate the four US plants to reduce fixed overhead and SG&A
Pursue growth in the aftermarket segment where High Q's quality advantage is a stronger differentiator
Diversify into plastic injection-molded parts for other industries (e.g., consumer goods, medical) to reduce dependence on price-competitive automotive OEM customers
Deepen the Toyota relationship, given Toyota's strong Truck/SUV market share growth through 2014
